The China Shock data — a guide

Diversity in a Globalized World

Published

September 9, 2026

What this data is about

In the 1990s and 2000s, China went from making very little for the world market to making a great deal of it. American factories that made the same things — clothes, furniture, toys, electronics — suddenly had a competitor.

But this did not happen evenly across the United States. A town whose factories made furniture felt it strongly. A town that grew wheat barely noticed. Two economists, David Autor and David Dorn, together with Gordon Hanson, measured how hard each part of the country was hit, and then measured what happened to jobs there.

This folder contains their data, cleaned up so you can work with it directly.

You are not expected to download anything, clean anything, or join anything together. That is done. You open a file and start looking.

The two files

There are two files, and they hold the same information in two different shapes. Which one you use depends on whether you are drawing a map or a graph.

File Use it for What one row is Rows
zones.rds Maps, and most graphs One place, one time period 1,444
jobs.rds Comparing men and women One place, one period, one sex 2,792

zones.rds carries 44 variables. jobs.rds is a smaller, reshaped slice of the same data, built so that men and women sit in separate rows and can be compared directly.

How to open them

Put both files in a folder called preprocessed_data next to your .qmd file, then:

library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

zones <- readRDS("preprocessed_data/zones.rds")
jobs  <- readRDS("preprocessed_data/jobs.rds")

That is all. No read.csv, no file paths to fight with, no packages to install beyond the ones you used in class.

First, what is a “zone”?

The data is not organised by city or by state. It is organised by commuting zone — a group of towns close enough together that people live in one and work in another.

This is a better unit than a city for our purposes. If the factory in your town closes, you might find work two towns over without moving house. A commuting zone is roughly “the area where you could realistically look for a job.”

The continental United States has 722 of them. Every zone has a number, called zone_id.

zones.rds — the main file

Each row is one commuting zone in one time period. Since there are 722 zones and two periods, there are 1,444 rows — every zone appears twice.

That matters for maps. If you draw a map without choosing a period, R will try to draw each zone twice on top of itself. So pick a period first:

nineties <- zones[zones$period == "1990-2000", ]

ggplot(nineties) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = import_competition), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "sqrt", name = "Import\ncompetition") +
  theme_void()

Swap import_competition for any variable below and you get a different map.

Where and when

Variable What it means
zone_id The zone’s ID number
state_fips State code
region Northeast, Midwest, South or West
period 1990-2000 or 2000-2007
geom The shape on the map — you never touch this directly

How hard China hit

Variable What it means
import_competition Chinese imports arriving in this zone’s industries. Bigger = hit harder
import_competition_other The same thing, but measured from China’s exports to other rich countries. Economists use this as a cleaner comparison

What the zone looked like at the start

All of these are measured at the beginning of the period.

Variable What it means
population How many people lived there
manuf_share_start % of jobs in factories
college_share % of adults with a college degree
foreign_born_share % of people born outside the US
female_empl_share % of workers who were women
routine_jobs_share % of jobs that were repetitive and rule-based
mfg_start % of jobs that were factory jobs
mfg_start_women / mfg_start_men The same, for women only / men only
mfg_start_college / mfg_start_nocollege The same, by education
unemployed_start % of people unemployed
not_in_labour_start % of people not looking for work at all
wage_mfg_start / wage_nonmfg_start Typical weekly pay, in factories / outside them

What changed over the period

Variable What it means
mfg_change Change in % of jobs that were factory jobs
mfg_change_women / mfg_change_men The same, by sex
mfg_change_college / mfg_change_nocollege The same, by education
nonmfg_change Change in non-factory employment
nonmfg_change_women / nonmfg_change_men The same, by sex
unemployed_change Change in % unemployed
unemployed_change_women / _men The same, by sex
not_in_labour_change Change in % who stopped looking for work
not_in_labour_change_women / _men The same, by sex
wage_change Change in typical weekly pay
wage_change_women / wage_change_men The same, by sex
population_change Change in population
household_income_change Change in average household income per person

Government payments

When people lose work, government money often follows. These track it.

Variable What it means
disability_recipients_change Change in % of people on disability benefits
disability_payments_change Change in disability money paid per person
unemployment_payments_change Change in unemployment money paid per person
trade_adjustment_payments_change Change in Trade Adjustment Assistance — money paid specifically to workers who lost jobs to imports

jobs.rds — for comparing men and women

In zones.rds, men and women sit in separate columns. That is awkward if you want them as two coloured lines on one graph. jobs.rds is the same data reshaped so they sit in separate rows, with a sex column saying which is which.

Variable What it means
zone_id, region, period Same as in zones.rds

A graph also takes one line:

ggplot(jobs, aes(x = import_competition, y = mfg_change, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_minimal()

The one thing that will confuse you

mfg_change and mfg_change_share_of_start sound like the same thing. They are not, and the difference matters more than anything else in this data.

Imagine a zone where women held 7% of the jobs in factories and men held 15%. Both groups then lose 3 percentage points.

  • In mfg_change, both lose the same: −3 each.
  • In mfg_change_share_of_start, women lost 3 out of 7, which is −43%. Men lost 3 out of 15, which is −20%.

Same event, two numbers, two impressions. mfg_change tells you how much the local job market shifted. mfg_change_share_of_start tells you how much of that group’s own work disappeared.

Neither is wrong. But your conclusion can flip depending on which one you use, so say which one you chose and why.

Things worth knowing

import_competition is very lopsided. Most zones have small values and a few have very large ones. On a plain map almost everything comes out the same colour. If that happens, add trans = "sqrt" inside scale_fill_viridis_c().

Bigger import_competition means hit harder, and most change values are negative because factory jobs were disappearing everywhere. So a downward-sloping line means “more competition went with bigger losses.”

We removed a few zones where almost nobody worked in factories to begin with. Dividing by a tiny starting number produced percentages in the hundreds, which are technically correct and practically meaningless.

Every zone appears twice in zones.rds — once per period. Filter to one period before mapping, or the two will be drawn on top of each other.

wage_change is a log change, so roughly: 0.05 means about 5% higher pay.

Questions you could ask

These are starting points, not a list to work through.

  • Which regions were hit hardest, and does that match where factory work was?
  • When factory jobs disappeared, did non-factory jobs replace them (nonmfg_change), or did people stop looking for work (not_in_labour_change)?
  • Did places hit harder end up with more people on disability benefits (disability_recipients_change)? That is a well-known and contested claim.
  • Did trade_adjustment_payments_change actually rise where imports hit hardest — did the money meant for these workers reach them?
  • Were places with more immigrants (foreign_born_share) hit more or less?
  • Did zones with more routine_jobs_share suffer more?
  • Did college and non-college workers fare differently (mfg_change_college vs mfg_change_nocollege)?
  • Do men and women show the same pattern, and does your answer depend on which of the two change measures you use?

Where the data comes from

Autor, D. H., Dorn, D., & Hanson, G. H. (2013). The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States. American Economic Review, 103(6), 2121–2168.

The replication files are public, on David Dorn’s website. Map boundaries come from the US Census Bureau. We joined them together, renamed the variables into plain English, and rounded the numbers.
